hints: Focus on atomic numbers first, a positive ion loses electrons while a negative ion gains them.
Sodium has atomic number 11, so its 1+ ion must have one fewer electron than the atom.
Each nitrogen has 7 electrons, so add up three nitrogens and then add one more for the 1- charge on $\text{N}_3^-$.
walkthrough:
**Count electrons in the sodium ion**

Sodium atom has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. To form $\text{Na}^+$, it loses one electron.

$$11 - 1 = 10 \text{ electrons in } \text{Na}^+$$

**Count electrons in neutral $\text{N}_3$**

Nitrogen has atomic number 7, so each N atom has 7 electrons. Three N atoms together have:

$$3 \times 7 = 21 \text{ electrons}$$

**Adjust for the charge on azide**

The azide ion is $\text{N}_3^-$, with a 1- charge. That means one extra electron has been gained compared to neutral.

$$21 + 1 = 22 \text{ electrons in } \text{N}_3^-$$

**Match to the table**

Sodium ion has 10 electrons and azide ion has 22 electrons. That combination is the correct row.

options.A: Sodium ion with 10 electrons is correct, but 20 for azide is wrong. This counts only $3 \times 7 = 21$ minus one, or forgets the extra electron for the 1- charge. Remember negative ions gain electrons.
options.B: This is correct. $\text{Na}^+$ has $11-1=10$ electrons, and $\text{N}_3^-$ has $(3 \times 7)+1=22$ electrons. Both ions end up isoelectronic with neon.
options.C: Both numbers are wrong. 12 is the electron count for a neutral Mg atom, not $\text{Na}^+$. Sodium loses an electron to get 10, it does not gain one to get 12.
options.D: Azide with 22 electrons is correct, but 12 for sodium is wrong. This is a common trap of adding the charge instead of subtracting it for a positive ion. $\text{Na}^+$ means lose one electron from 11 to give 10.
